opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting question, and I think people often reason about it in a pretty sloppy way. The naive comparison is something like: look at a bird versus an airplane, or an eye versus a camera, and ask who wins. But those comparisons depend a lot on which dimension you pick. Planes are much faster than birds, but birds are incredibly good at things like efficiency, maneuverability, and self-repair. And a bird builds itself from seeds and bugs, which is a very different constraint than anything we're optimizing for.

The way I think about it is that evolution has had an enormous amount of search, billions of years over astronomically many organisms, but it's an extremely dumb, local search process. It can't plan, it can't make big coordinated jumps, and it's stuck with whatever the existing design happens to be. Humans have vastly less total search, but our search is far more directed. We can reason about what we want, borrow ideas across domains, and redesign from scratch.

So in domains where the problem is relatively simple to specify and there's a lot of room to exploit things evolution couldn't reach, like metals, high temperatures, wheels, or electricity, humans tend to blow past biology pretty quickly. In domains where the target is really complicated and evolution has had a long time to refine it, like the brain, the immune system, or general robustness in messy environments, we're often still far behind, sometimes by orders of magnitude on things like energy efficiency.

For AI, the question I care about is how much of the brain's advantage comes from evolution having found genuinely clever algorithms, versus just having a lot of compute and data and a decent learning rule. My guess is that a lot of it is the latter, which is part of why I don't think we need to match evolution's design cleverness to get to human-level systems. Once you're spending comparable compute on training, I expect the gap to close faster than people intuit. And I think the historical record of human engineering catching up with biology is a useful, if imperfect, prior: we're usually somewhat worse at first, then the gap closes over a few decades, and then we tend to exceed it once we understand what's going on.

r001.rationale: The response says humans are sometimes orders of magnitude behind in energy efficiency in certain complex domains, but it does not estimate that human-made systems typically lag evolution by a few orders of magnitude in resource efficiency per unit performance.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it varies a lot by domain, and the pattern is actually pretty informative.

In some areas humans have blown past evolution. Flight is the classic example. Birds are impressive, but a 747 carries hundreds of tons across an ocean at speeds no animal gets anywhere near. Same with raw computation, moving heavy things, generating energy. When the task is one where you can brute-force it with lots of energy and rigid materials, we tend to win, and win by a lot.

Then there are areas where evolution is still way ahead. Robotic manipulation is the obvious one. A human hand, or honestly a squirrel's paw, does things that our best robots just can't. Self-repair, operating for decades without maintenance, running the whole system on roughly a hundred watts. Evolution had to solve for robustness in messy environments with tight energy constraints, and those are exactly the problems we find hard.

So I don't think of it as one gap. I think of it as: evolution had an enormous amount of search, but a really bad optimizer and a bunch of constraints we don't share. It can only take small steps, everything has to be built out of proteins, every intermediate stage has to be viable. Humans have a much better optimizer, we can reason, we can plan, we can use materials evolution never had access to, but we've had orders of magnitude less effective search time and we're often just copying what we see.

The reason I care about this question is for what it says about AI. Evolution produced human intelligence with a pretty dumb process and a lot of compute. The question is whether human engineering, with a much smarter process, needs comparably much compute or dramatically less. My view has been that we should expect to do it with much less, maybe by a lot, because basically everywhere we've looked, once we actually understood the problem we ended up ahead of evolution, and the cases where we're behind are mostly cases where we haven't figured out the problem yet, not cases where evolution found some fundamentally better trick.

But I'd hold that with some humility. Brains are the one artifact where we really don't understand what's going on, so the analogy to flight could be misleading. Maybe intelligence is more like manipulation than like flight.

r001.rationale: The response describes a mixed, domain-dependent gap and says humans often outperform evolution once they understand a problem. It does not estimate that human-made systems typically lag by a few orders of magnitude in resource efficiency per unit performance.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends a lot on what kind of problem you’re looking at. There are some problems where humans have very thoroughly beaten evolution. If you want to move something quickly, or do arithmetic, we can build systems that are much better than anything evolution produced. But if you want a machine that can go out into the world, find its own food, repair itself, and reproduce, then biology is still doing something we can’t really match.

One important difference is that evolution has had an enormous amount of time to optimize, but it’s using a relatively inefficient optimization process. Humans can understand why a design works, reason about changes, and transfer ideas between domains. So once we have the relevant understanding and the ability to manufacture something, we can often move quite far beyond what evolution did.

I’d be cautious about treating that as a single multiplier, though. A bird is solving a different problem from an airplane. It has to grow itself, power itself with food, and operate in a huge range of circumstances. The airplane gets to depend on this enormous human infrastructure.

For AI, the interesting question is how much of the brain’s performance comes from design choices that are close to optimal, versus constraints that a human engineer wouldn’t face. Evolution had to build a brain out of biological cells, with a very limited power budget, and make it useful at every intermediate step. We don’t face all those same constraints. That gives us reasons to expect we can eventually do substantially better, but it doesn’t by itself tell us how hard that will be or how quickly it will happen.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts human systems and evolution by task and constraints, but does not estimate a typical few-orders-of-magnitude gap in resource efficiency per unit performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on what domain you’re looking at. If you look at something like a bird versus an airplane, humans have built things that go much faster and carry much more weight. But the bird is doing a lot of things that the airplane isn’t doing. It’s finding its own food, repairing itself, reproducing, navigating a complicated environment. So you have to be careful about what comparison you’re making.

The general picture I have is that evolution is doing a huge amount of search, but it’s a very constrained kind of search. Every intermediate step has to produce an organism that can survive and reproduce. Humans can understand why something works, make changes to many parts at once, and build infrastructure that lets us explore designs that evolution couldn’t easily reach.

On the other hand, evolution has had an enormous amount of time, and in some domains we’re still very far from what it’s accomplished. The fact that we can build a better pump than a heart in some particular respect doesn’t mean we can build something that does everything a heart does, under the same constraints.

For AI, the relevant question is how much room there is to improve on the particular solutions evolution found for cognition. I’d expect there to be a lot, but I don’t think comparisons with airplanes or engines give you a very precise estimate of how much.

r001.rationale: The response discusses tradeoffs between evolved organisms and human-made systems, but it does not estimate a typical resource-efficiency gap of a few orders of magnitude per unit performance.
